question.prompt: Let \[f(x)=\sum_{k=2}^{10}(\lfloor kx \rfloor -k \lfloor x \rfloor),\] where \(\lfloor r \rfloor\) denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to \(r.\) How many distinct values does \(f(x)\) assume for \(x \ge 0?\)

solutions.explanation:
First separate the integer and fractional parts of \(x\). Write
\[
x=n+t,\qquad n=\lfloor x\rfloor,\qquad 0\le t<1.
\]
For each integer \(k\), the number \(kn\) is an integer, so
\[
\lfloor kx\rfloor=kn+\lfloor kt\rfloor.
\]
Consequently,
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=2}^{10}\lfloor kt\rfloor.
\]
Every \(t\in[0,1)\) occurs by taking \(x=t\), so we only need to count the values of this sum on that interval.

Each term \(\lfloor kt\rfloor\) stays constant until \(t\) reaches one of
\[
\frac1k,\frac2k,\ldots,\frac{k-1}{k},
\]
where it increases by 1. No term decreases. Thus the sum strictly increases at every distinct location in this collection. Some terms jump together, so counting all individual jumps would overcount the number of locations.

Reduce each fraction to lowest terms. The distinct locations are exactly the fractions \(p/q\) with \(1\le p<q\le10\) and no common factor between \(p\) and \(q\). Indeed, reducing \(j/k\) leaves a denominator at most \(k\le10\); conversely, every such \(p/q\) is a jump of the term \(\lfloor qt\rfloor\). Unique reduced forms prevent double counting.

For the prime denominators \(2,3,5,7\), every numerator from 1 through \(q-1\) works, giving respectively \(1,2,4,6\) locations. For denominators 4 and 8, exactly the odd numerators work, giving 2 and 4. For denominator 6, only 1 and 5 work, giving 2. For denominator 9, omit 3 and 6, giving 6. For denominator 10, the allowed numerators are 1, 3, 7, and 9, giving 4. The total is
\[
1+2+4+6+2+4+2+6+4=31.
\]
There is one initial value, 0, before the first jump, followed by one new value at each of the 31 locations. At a jump, the floor values already equal their values immediately to the right, so the endpoints add no extra values. The endpoint \(t=1\) is excluded; integer inputs instead have fractional part 0. Therefore the number of distinct values is
\[
31+1=\boxed{32},
\]
choice \(\boxed{A}\).
solutions.title: Count distinct places where the sum increases
